desc:
Return the node values of a binary tree in postorder: everything in the left subtree (in postorder), then everything in the right subtree (in postorder), and the node itself last. The empty tree gives the empty array.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] the answer is [4, 2, 3, 1]. For tree = [5, 8, 2, 7, -1, 4, 9] the answer is [7, 8, 4, 9, 2, 5].

The recursive version is trivial. Solve it iteratively, with an explicit stack and without recursion.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: A node is recorded only after both of its subtrees are finished, which makes the iterative version trickier than for preorder.
Look at the mirror of preorder: visiting node, then right subtree, then left subtree. How does this sequence relate to postorder?
Postorder is exactly the reverse of “node, right, left”. Run the iterative preorder with the two pushes swapped (push left first, then right) and reverse the result.
editorial: Reverse the postorder sequence (left, right, node) and you get (node, right, left). That is a preorder in which the right child is explored before the left child, which a stack handles easily: pop a node, record it, push its left child, then push its right child (so the right child is popped first). At the end reverse the recorded list.

The cost is O(n) time and O(n) space. A single-stack alternative keeps a pointer to the last visited node and records a node only when its right child is missing or was just visited; it saves the final reversal but is much easier to get wrong, so the reversal trick is the better choice in an interview.
